title.official: Notice to obtain record of proceedings

subdivision.heading: Additional Rules Specific to Originating Applications for Judicial Review

operative_text.controlling:
3.18(1)  An originating applicant for judicial review who seeks an
order to set aside a decision or act must include with the originating
application a notice in Form 8, addressed to the person or body
who made or possesses the record of proceedings on which the
decision or act sought to be set aside is based, to send the record of
proceedings to the court clerk named in the notice.
(2)  The notice must require the following to be sent or an
explanation to be provided of why an item cannot be sent:
(a) the written record, if any, of the decision or act that is the
subject of the originating application for judicial review,
(b) the reasons given for the decision or act, if any,
(c) the document which started the proceeding,
(d) the evidence and exhibits filed with the person or body, if
any, and
(e) anything else relevant to the decision or act in the
possession of the person or body.
(3)  The Court may add to, dispense with or vary anything required
to be sent to the court clerk under this rule.

BOOK_A.defined_terms: Court, court clerk At one time, the writ ofcertiorarihad two effects.First, it immediately moved the record (both physically, and notionally the whole proceeding) from the inferior body to the superior court.And second, it led to a hearing at which the superior court would examine the record and ultimately decide whether or not to quash the decision below.The first of those two effects is now covered by Rules 3.18 ff. Where the Originating Application seeks to set aside a decision or act, the applicant has the right and duty to have the inferior body physically send up its record to King's Bench.That is demanded by a special endorsement on the Originating Application, and its service on the inferior body.Where the Originating Application does not seek to set aside a decision, but some other relief (e.g.prohibition), R.3.20 allows King's Bench to order the record below sent up. Generally speaking, the scope of relevance for the return is broad, and is not confined to matters listed in R.3.18(2). BOOK_B.title: Notice to obtain record of proceedings

commentary.text: Rule 3.18 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.18. What Constitutes the Record? In Alberta, the constitution of the record is set out in rules 753.12 and 753.13(1) of the Rules of Court… What is included in the record is not definitive due to the phrases “all things touching the matter” in rules 753.12(1), 753.13(1) and “all other papers or documents touching the matter” in rule 753.13(1)(d). In these two rules the words, “all things” or “all papers or documents” are qualified by the words “touching the matter”. Broda v. Edmonton (City) (1989), 102 A.R. 255 (Q.B.), at 258, per Trussler J. And Smith J. said: As was held by Miller J. in A.U.P.E. v. Alberta, [1978] 3 W.W.R. 63 (T.D.), the effect of R. 753.12 and 753.13 is to expand the constituent elements of the record: It seems abundantly clear that Rules 743 and 744 [now R. 753.12 and 753.13] were specifically worded to eliminate the restrictions laid down in the Nat Bell case by broadening the material required to be placed before the reviewing court and placed an obligation on the latter tribunal to examine the evidence wherever relevant to the application. However, Miller J. further qualified the scope of these two rules at p. 7 by stating: It seems to me that the logical way of interpreting the wording of Rules 743 and 744 is that the inferior tribunal should only be compelled to produce what they already have on hand at the time of the certiorari application or that which they are specifically required to produce by statute, regulation or agreement. Alberta (Labour Relations Board) v. I.B.E.W., Local 1007 (1991), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 253 at 260 (Q.B.).
